title: Fixing a twisted foundation chain
subtitle: Why the first row curls under, and what to do about it
excerpt: A twisted foundation chain — where the chain spirals instead of lying flat — is one of the most common problems on a first project. It usually appears after the first few rows when the twist becomes visible. The fix depends on how far you have got.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — troubleshooting first rows. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet.

glossaryTerms.definition: A foundation chain that has rotated around its own axis before joining or before the first row of stitches is complete, causing the piece to spiral. Usually caused by the chain turning as it hangs below the hook.

The smooth side of the foundation chain, showing a row of even V-shapes. The foundation chain has two faces: the smooth V-face (worked from) and the bumped back. Keeping the V-face consistently facing the same direction prevents a twist.

heroPrompt: A short crochet swatch showing a clearly twisted foundation chain causing the piece to spiral, next to an untwisted flat piece of the same size — both in cream DK cotton on a pale background.

content.text: is exactly what it sounds like: the chain has rotated along its length before you have finished the first row. The result is a piece that spirals or folds rather than lying flat. It is almost always invisible at the end of a long foundation chain — the twist only becomes obvious once a few rows are worked and the fabric tightens.
After making the foundation chain, hold it between your hands and look at the

— the row of V-shapes should all face the same way along the full length. If the V-shapes rotate or flip at any point, the chain is twisted. Correct it before starting row 1 by gently unspinning the chain from the tail end.
After every 15-20 chains, stop and look at the chain face. If it is still showing V-shapes consistently, continue. If it has started to rotate, untwist before adding more chains.
Let the chain hang freely between your hands before starting row 1 — gravity will settle the chain into its natural orientation. If it rotates as it hangs, there is already a twist.
If you only discover it after row 1

For a flat piece: the twist cannot be corrected without frogging back to the foundation chain. Frog row 1, untwist the chain, and re-work the row. For a circular piece (ring worked in rounds): in most cases the work will still lie flat because the circle closes itself. Check by holding the circle flat — if it lies flat, the twist isn't a problem. If it folds or figures-of-eight, frog and re-work.

attrs.title: Long chains are more prone to twisting
attrs.body: On a chain of 200 stitches for a large blanket, the weight of the chain pulling down as you make it almost always introduces some rotation. After completing the chain, lay it on a flat surface and check it before starting row 1. Untwisting a laid-flat chain is easier than untwisting a hanging chain.
